proposal.description_long: The Justice Department filed suit in October 1973 in the Eastern District of New York against Donald Trump, his father Fred Trump, and Trump Management, alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act across 39 buildings containing more than 14,000 apartments. The Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse case file says the complaint relied in part on paired testing: white testers were told about vacancies while Black testers were not or were steered to different properties. It also alleged employees used codes beside applicants’ names to indicate race. The defendants counterclaimed for defamation; the court dismissed that counterclaim and allowed the federal case to proceed. The parties resolved the case through a consent decree signed June 10, 1975. It barred discrimination in rental terms and practices, required Donald and Fred Trump to familiarize themselves with the Act, and required advertisements stating that minorities had equal opportunity to apply. Trump Management also had to provide the New York Urban League weekly vacancy lists for two years. The decree expressly stated that it was not an admission of a violation. The record supports the filing, allegations, and negotiated obligations, but not a claim that a court found the defendants liable.

proposal.description_long: The American Association of People with Disabilities (AAPD) published a policy brief on October 29, 2024, describing Project 2025 proposals affecting Medicaid and disability services. AAPD says the plan would convert Medicaid toward block-grant or per-capita funding and limit home- and community-based services (HCBS), which many people with disabilities use to live independently. AAPD argues that these funding and eligibility changes could restrict supports and coverage; that is the organization’s assessment of proposed policy. The assigned sources do not establish that the Trump administration abolished ADA accommodations, eliminated ADA enforcement, implemented the Medicaid cuts described in the former long text, or forced disabled people into institutions. Nor do they establish a realized coverage-loss count. This entry is therefore narrowed to the documented advocacy warning about proposals and potential consequences, with attribution made explicit. It should not present projected harms as completed government action or describe all accommodations and community-living protections as already eliminated.

preserved_fields.description_long: Donald Trump systematically eliminated disability rights protections by gutting Americans with Disabilities Act enforcement, ending Medicaid funding that enabled community living, and removing 'disparate impact' discrimination protections that had addressed systemic ableism while forcing disabled Americans back into institutional settings through funding cuts and accommodation elimination. The comprehensive disability rights destruction represented Trump's implementation of Project 2025's plan to eliminate federal regulations and programs that supported independent living, with $880 billion in Medicaid cuts that would 'strip coverage from 17 million people' including disabled Americans who relied on federal healthcare for wheelchairs, ventilators, personal care attendants, and community-based services. The ADA rollback included eliminating 'disparate impact' discrimination protections that addressed unintentional but systematic bias against disabled people, while removing federal requirements for businesses, educational institutions, and government agencies to provide reasonable accommodations that ensured equal access and participation. Trump's disability targeting violated constitutional equal protection principles by removing legal tools that disabled Americans used to 'highlight ableism within institutions' and seek redress for discrimination, while Medicaid cuts forced disabled people 'out of their homes and into hospitals and nursing homes' against their will and constitutional rights. The disability rights elimination created what advocates called return to 'earlier, shameful era of isolation, exclusion, and institutionalization' by removing Olmstead protections that affirmed disabled people's right to live in community settings with appropriate supports rather than segregated institutional facilities. The systematic accommodation destruction represented Project 2025's vision of society that abandoned federal responsibility for disability inclusion, transforming disabled Americans from equal citizens with supported rights into vulnerable populations subject to institutional control and social exclusion through elimination of legal protections and community-based services.

proposal.description_long: The Guardian’s May 27, 2025 report describes a dispute over a purported warrantless wiretap during the Pentagon’s investigation into classified-information leaks. According to advisers quoted by the newspaper, Tim Parlatore, Pete Hegseth’s personal lawyer and a supervisor of the inquiry, suggested investigators had found a warrantless wiretap on an aide’s phone. The report says Parlatore later denied that a wiretap had occurred and that White House advisers regarded the claim as untrue. The Guardian also reported that the inquiry moved to Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg’s office around the time Parlatore planned to step away. These accounts support a headline about conflicting reports and the handling of the investigation. A New York Times report published May 22 described potential target categories, including energy facilities, an underground nuclear-storage site at Isfahan, and missile sites, if Trump chose to resume attacks. proposal.description_long: NBC News reported that in the final hours of his first presidency, Donald Trump granted clemency to 143 people: 73 received pardons and 70 had sentences commuted. Former White House adviser Steve Bannon was among those pardoned. The article says Bannon had been indicted with three others on conspiracy charges involving wire fraud and money laundering related to the “We Build the Wall” crowdfunding campaign. Prosecutors alleged that hundreds of thousands of dollars in donations were diverted for personal expenses; Bannon had not been tried on those charges when he received clemency, so the allegations were not resolved at trial. NBC separately notes that Trump had pardoned Michael Flynn and Roger Stone and commuted Paul Manafort’s sentence earlier, rather than including all three in this final-hours group. The reported 143 figure therefore covers different forms of clemency and does not support describing every recipient as an ally or every grant as a pardon. The revised title keeps Bannon’s pardon and the group total while distinguishing pardons from commutations, prior grants, and unresolved criminal allegations.
proposal.description_medium: The January 20, 2021 clemency statement says President Donald Trump pardoned 73 people and commuted the sentences of 70 others in his final hours in office. It specifically lists a full pardon for Steve Bannon, who faced federal charges related to the We Build the Wall fundraising effort. The statement does not show that all 143 recipients were allies, and Flynn, Stone and Manafort received clemency earlier.
